questions.statement: Choose the correct quantifier: 'There aren't ___ students in the classroom today.'
questions.context: Semana W23 de ingles, grado 11: ejercicio 1 de 20 sobre quantifiers some, any, much and many.

options.text: any
options.feedback: Correct! In a negative sentence 'any' is used to mean 'none at all', which matches the negative 'aren't'.

options.text: some
options.feedback: No. 'Some' normally appears in affirmative or inviting sentences, not after a negative auxiliary.

options.text: much
options.feedback: No. 'Much' is for uncountable nouns, and students are countable.

options.text: a few
options.feedback: No. 'A few' states that a small positive number exists, which contradicts 'aren't'.

questions.explanation:
In a negative sentence 'any' is used to mean 'none at all', which matches the negative 'aren't'. In this item the choice that works is 'any', because it is the option that matches what the sentence and the task require.

questions.statement: Which quantifier correctly completes the question: '___ milk is left in the fridge?'
questions.context: Semana W23 de ingles, grado 11: ejercicio 2 de 20 sobre quantifiers some, any, much and many.

options.text: How much
options.feedback: Correct! Milk is uncountable, so the question about its quantity is built with 'how much'.

options.text: How many
options.feedback: No. 'How many' is for countable plural nouns, and milk cannot be counted.

options.text: How few
options.feedback: No. 'How few' would ask about a countable plural noun in a negative sense.

options.text: How long
options.feedback: No. 'How long' asks about duration or length, not about the amount of a substance.

questions.explanation:
Milk is uncountable, so the question about its quantity is built with 'how much'. In this item the choice that works is 'How much', because it is the option that matches what the sentence and the task require.

questions.statement: Choose the sentence with the correct quantifier.
questions.context: Semana W23 de ingles, grado 11: ejercicio 3 de 20 sobre quantifiers some, any, much and many.

options.text: We have much work to finish before Friday.
options.feedback: Correct! 'Work' is uncountable here, so 'much' is the quantifier that matches it.

options.text: We have many work to finish before Friday.
options.feedback: No. 'Many' is for countable plural nouns, and uncountable 'work' takes 'much'.

options.text: We have a many work to finish before Friday.
options.feedback: No. 'A many' is not a valid combination; the article cannot precede 'many' in this sense.

options.text: We have much works to finish before Friday.
options.feedback: No. 'Works' would make the noun countable, which changes the meaning of the sentence.

questions.explanation:
'Work' is uncountable here, so 'much' is the quantifier that matches it. In this item the choice that works is 'We have much work to finish before Friday.', because it is the option that matches what the sentence and the task require.

questions.statement: Which sentence is correct when offering something with 'some'?
questions.context: Semana W23 de ingles, grado 11: ejercicio 4 de 20 sobre quantifiers some, any, much and many.

options.text: Would you like some coffee before the class?
options.feedback: Correct! 'Some' is the usual quantifier in an offer, which is exactly the use being tested here.

options.text: Would you like any coffee before the class?
options.feedback: No. 'Any' belongs to negative and interrogative contexts, and an offer is neither of those.

options.text: Would you like much coffee before the class?
options.feedback: No. 'Much' would imply a large amount, which is not what an offer asks about.

options.text: Would you like a coffee before the class?
options.feedback: No. 'A coffee' is possible but the question asks about the quantifier, and 'some' is the natural offer form.

questions.explanation:
'Some' is the usual quantifier in an offer, which is exactly the use being tested here. In this item the choice that works is 'Would you like some coffee before the class?', because it is the option that matches what the sentence and the task require.

questions.context: Semana W23 de ingles, grado 11: ejercicio 5 de 20 sobre quantifiers some, any, much and many.

options.text: many
options.feedback: Correct! 'Apples' is a countable plural noun, so the question about quantity takes 'how many'.

options.text: much

options.text: little
options.feedback: No. 'Little' can quantify a countable plural only as 'how few'; 'how little' measures an uncountable amount.

options.text: long
options.feedback: No. 'Long' asks about length or duration and never about the number of apples.

'Apples' is a countable plural noun, so the question about quantity takes 'how many'. In this item the choice that works is 'many', because it is the option that matches what the sentence and the task require.

options.text: There is not much space on the desk and there are not many chairs around it.

options.text: There is not much space on the desk and there are not much chairs around it.
options.feedback: No. 'Much chairs' is the second half of the sentence; the countable plural 'chairs' require 'many'.

options.text: There is not many space on the desk and there are not many chairs around it.
options.feedback: No. 'Many space' is the first half of the sentence; the uncountable noun 'space' requires 'much'.

questions.explanation:
Uncountable 'space' takes 'much' and countable plural 'chairs' take 'many', each with its own quantifier. questions.statement: Which sentence uses 'any' correctly in a negative sentence with an uncountable noun?
questions.context: Semana W23 de ingles, grado 11: ejercicio 7 de 20 sobre quantifiers some, any, much and many.

options.text: We do not have any time left before the exam.
options.feedback: Correct! 'Any' is the quantifier used after a negative auxiliary to mean 'none of it at all'.

options.text: We do not have some time left before the exam.
options.feedback: No. 'Some' in a negative sentence would suggest that a little does exist, which contradicts 'do not have'.

options.text: We do not have much time left before the exam.
options.feedback: No. 'Much' would be right after 'how' or 'so', but after 'do not have' the neutral form is 'any'.

options.text: We do not have a time left before the exam.
options.feedback: No. 'A time' would name a single occasion rather than the amount of time available.

questions.explanation:
'Any' is the quantifier used after a negative auxiliary to mean 'none of it at all'. In this item the choice that works is 'We do not have any time left before the exam.', because it is the option that matches what the sentence and the task require.

options.text: There are a few questions I still need to review.
options.feedback: Correct! 'A few' states that some but not many countable items exist, which matches the plural 'questions'.

options.text: There are a few question I still need to review.
options.feedback: No. 'A few question' is singular, but 'a few' must be followed by a plural noun.

options.text: There are few questions I still need to review, and they are none.
options.feedback: No. 'Few' without an article already means almost none, and 'none' contradicts it outright.

options.text: There are a few water I still need to review.
options.feedback: No. 'A few water' pairs a countable quantifier with an uncountable noun.

questions.explanation:
'A few' states that some but not many countable items exist, which matches the plural 'questions'. In this item the choice that works is 'There are a few questions I still need to review.', because it is the option that matches what the sentence and the task require.

options.text: Much of my classmates work part time on weekends.
options.feedback: No. 'Much' is for uncountable nouns, and 'classmates' is a countable plural.

options.text: A some of my classmates work part time on weekends.
options.feedback: No. 'A some' is not a valid combination; an article cannot be added to 'some' in this use.

questions.explanation:
